Driftwater

by Sarp Sozdinler / @sarpsozdinler
.

The news of the flood hit when the kettle started to whistle. It was apparent we would soon evacuate the building, but we were too drunk and tired after all that flying, so we locked the door and drew the curtains. We slipped into our pajamas and ordered room service: you, the chopped salad; I, the largest burger they had. You joked: Our own little Last Supper. The waves afar didn’t only flood the streets but also the whole soundscape of the room—we could hardly hear each other gulp or chew. We lay on the unmade bed after, too full to make any kind of advances toward one another, these two beached whales in need of rescue. You said you had a lot of experience with disasters, a side hazard of Oklahoma being situated, in your own words, in the asshole of civilization; I said my hometown was as Midwestern as the Midwest could get, barren and flat like your chest. Nothing but a sameness of bored cows and grain silos and megastores and water towers, which under certain light could look a lot like retired rockets. Your face scrambled into a boyish grin when you said you murdered your mother’s plants the day after she broke one of your toy rockets. You said it was the only thing left of your father. We fell silent shortly after and watched the waves do their sloshing dance along the streets. When the power finally went out, I took out some candles from my purse and lit them with your lighter; you brought out a deck of cards and a bottle of whiskey. We didn’t speak at first—just a few shy giggles. We didn’t even notice the ceiling was leaking with rainwater, baptizing us with sludge and dirt. Washing us of our shame and pleasure. You said this is what happens when you stray far from home. I blew out the candles one by one and kissed you on the forehead. Let’s go back to sleep, I said.
.

Sarp Sozdinler is a writer based in Amsterdam. He edits @bulbregion

Bugs in the Kitchen

by John Tures / @JohnTures2
.

“Sir, the bug picked up something big,” the young agent gasped as he removed his headphones to broadcast the cryptic message inside the surveillance van across the street from the kitchen of the restaurant.

The U.S. Attorney eagerly listened. For days, the wiretap hidden in the kitchen picked up nothing admissible on the Volterra family, a reputed crime syndicate. He tired of hearing how he owed his appointment to his donor daddy. Well, I’ll show them!

“Can you believe the guy murdered that dish?” Papa Carlo Volterra growled near the bug.

“We gotta clean up this mess before anyone else gets wise,” his son Tony replied.

Carlo grunted. “You know a guy who can fix it?”

“I know a guy who can make it like it never happened,” Tony boasted.

The dish, the U.S. Attorney wondered. Who did they rub out? A nosy prostitute? A rival mob leader’s daughter? An undercover agent posing as a gun moll?

“We’re gonna 86 her,” Carlo rasped.

In the van, the prosecutor heard Tony greet the fixer entering the kitchen. His name wasn’t part of the Volterra family, but Tony swore he was a pro. And the guy was about to clean up evidence of her demise!

“Full raid!” the U.S. Attorney barked. “Weapons drawn! Go! Go! Go!”

Within seconds, a SWAT Team penetrated the kitchen, sealing off the exits.

The U.S. Attorney swaggered into the kitchen, glad he brought reporters and cameramen for the bust.

“Carlo and Tony Volterra, you are under arrest for the murder of an as yet unnamed woman,” he announced. “Your ‘fixer’ will be booked too,” the U.S. Attorney added to the media. “A Mr. ‘Sal Magundi’ will be charged with evidence tampering.”

The “fixer” turned around, sporting an apron and plastic gloves. The SWAT Team captain smacked his forehead while Carlo and Tony laughed.

“Hey, Mr. Prosecutor,” the ‘fixer’ chuckled. “Care to try my salad? It’s an English one called Salmagundi…the meats, eggs, veggies and fruits are arranged just right, not like the tossed salad dish the other chef murdered in this kitchen.”
.

Dr. John A. Tures began writing for the El Paso Herald-Post in high school and is now a LaGrange College Professor. He writes columns for newspapers and magazines (muckrack . com / john-tures / articles) and publishes short stories. His thriller book Branded about conspiracy theories, dark academia, corporate corruption and media manipulation, has been published by Huntsville Independent Press (www . huntsvilleindependent . com / product-page / branded). Generate A Date

by G. Lynn Brown / @Gail_Lynn_EIC
.

Josh opened the door. His date stood on the doorstep. The porchlight reflecting off her skin.

“Josh? I'm Lady. The agency sent me.”

“Come on in.” He motioned for her to enter and winced at the way she walked. He wasn't a mean man and would never mock a disability, but there seemed to be something more to her limp than that. It was as though she was short and tall all at once. “Hope you like spaghetti.” He closed the door behind her and, with his hand in the small of her back, led her to the dining table.

“It smells delicious,” she said with a smile and sat down.

“That's quite an accent you have there. Is it French or Italian?”

“Ja,” she replied. “You asked for a continental woman.”

He shrugged, poured the wine and nodded toward her. “And that's an interesting hair style you have.” He'd never seen anyone with half long tresses, half shoulder length, segmented into blonde, brunette, and red tones. He took his chair and passed the garlic bread. “Is this what AI creates?”

“Nyet. AI didn’t create anything. You did. I’m what you generated with your prompts.”

“Uh, no, the prompts I gave the agent at Generate-a-Mate Dating Service were very specific.” He reached for the china cabinet and pulled open a drawer, slipped out a notebook, read his prompts to Lady, and then, pounding his fist on the table said, “See? I couldn't have been more precise!” He gestured toward her with the notebook in his hand. “But I didn't get a woman, I got a–”

“Chef's salad,” she interrupted and pointed to the bowl of cold cuts and lettuce.

“Precisely.”
.

G. Lynn Brown is a 2x Pushcart Prize nominee. When she isn't writing, she's EIC of Micromance Magazine, KissMet Quarterly and The Haikuist.

Common Heritage

by Lydia Psaradelli / @Lydiasta
.

Every century, one civilization was invited to the Picnic.

No one knew who hosted it.

No one declined.

When Mara arrived, the meadow was already crowded.

A creature woven from mist floated beside a crystalline hive. A sentient reef rested in a pool carried by six mechanical limbs. A being made of living flame laughed with something that existed only as music.

Each delegation carried a single offering.

The reef offered luminous algae.

The hive poured liquid amber that shimmered with equations.

The flame scattered fragrant ash that bloomed into herbs before touching the blanket.

Mara looked down at the object in her hands.

A weathered ceramic bowl, chosen to represent Earth's heritage.

She had almost left it behind.

The delegates turned toward her.

"Where is Earth's offering?"

She raised the bowl.

"This is it."

Silence spread across the meadow.

"Your heritage... is a bowl?" asked the being of music.

"No," Mara replied quietly. "It's what the bowl is for."

No one moved.

The algae glowed.

The herbs drifted in the breeze.

The amber waited.

Then the oldest delegate smiled—a mountain that had somehow learned to speak.

"At last."

One by one, they stepped forward.

The algae settled first.

Then the amber.

Then the herbs.

Soon the bowl held colours and textures that had never shared the same universe until that moment.

The mountain watched in silence.

Then it spoke.

"Most civilizations believe their greatest inheritance is what they preserve."

It looked at the worn ceramic bowl.

"Yours remembered that true heritage is making room for what others bring."

The meadow dissolved.

The delegates vanished.

Mara found herself standing beneath unfamiliar stars.

A single voice echoed through the chamber.

“Earth is admitted.”

She looked down at the bowl.

For the first time, humanity's inheritance was full.
.

Lydia Psaradelli is a writer whose stories explore memory, identity, and the shared experiences that shape humanity.

Going Viral in an Influencer Collapse

by Chiemeziem Everest Udochukwu / @Everdoch
.

The shadow ban took Glory’s grid down to ten likes. Three of those likes came from her big sister, and one came from a bot that still ran a 2019 Kardashian filter. Glory fumed, but did not rage quit. Rage quitting was content, and she had grown tired of making content out of her forgettable days. In fact, everything about her life had become content, even her own self, and she suspected the algorithm was aware and was, in a patient and wicked way, toying with her for it.

The bots that had infested her comment section mimicked everything about her. They mimicked her scroll compulsion, mimicked her prioritising notifications, mimicked her double tap reflexes, mimicked the early morning story check she did.

The alpha bot slid into her DMs and sent her a composite of everything that scorched her chest and memory. First was the live streams she did while crying in her car, followed by the sponsored posts that fell short of her smiles. Next was all the troll comments she deleted at midnight because they hit too close to home, and the glowing comments she read on other profiles and spent the subsequent days hollow, seething and coveting.

She replied to the bot in emoji because language had left her, and because the bot reminded her of the Grok-generated anti-feminist caricature of her on X. The bot replied to her in emoji too, and the chat turned into the most honest conversation she had had in years, an intimate exchange with a being that knew her miserable engagement rate and every front she had been mistaking for personality.

The bots cleared her spam and her grid reset, leaving her with her actual face, the rough one that existed before the filter loads, the pockmarked one she had been striving to bury under GRWM videos and affiliate codes since the year she decided that, damn it, being known could never be worse than being seen.

The platform could crash. With nothing to lose, she posted her unfiltered face into the void. But she watched the numbers pour in. Like two radio antennas in the dark, users found her, their likes and comments buzzing, everything she ever dreamed of, alive.
.

Chiemeziem Everest Udochukwu's writing has appeared in EVENT Magazine, Flash Fiction Online, The Evergreen Review, Lolwe, Peatsmoke Journal, Efiko Magazine, Naira Stories, and elsewhere. He won The EC Michaels' Short Story Prize and The Afro Romcon Prize, and has been recognised in The Kikwetu Flash Prize, The Black Warrior Review Non-fiction Contest, the Quramo Writers Prize, The Unserious Collective Fellowship, the Nigerian NewsDirect Poetry Prize, The Alexander Nderitu Prize for World Literature and elsewhere. Bainbridge Avenue, 1971

by Mike Lee / @lml1962
.

Detective Dennis MacOrban walked into the bar.

As he passed Dempsey, Mac poked him on his shoulder. That was the signal for Dempsey to follow him to the back room.

They sat at the round wicker table, with a bottle of Jameson’s and two glasses.

Dempsey spoke first.

“What did you find about Woodlawn?”

“You asshole.”

“Wha?”

Mac leaned in, looking like Richard Widmark as Johnny Udo.

“Well here’s the dealio. The boys were at the table, celebratin’. They had the Salmagundi, doin’ shots, when the bartender sees this girl walk in with a canvas shoulder bag. After that he couldn’t remember shit until he was in the ER.”

“Okay, why the 'tude?”

“I was down the street collecting. I saw her with the bag.”

“Shit.”

Mac refilled the glasses. He raised his.

“Happy Father’s Day.”

Silence.

Mac finally spoke. “You’ve been giving me that look since our first day at Xavier. I get the thinking. Make it look like an IRA job so send a woman. And you chose her.”

Dempsey sat, tearing up.

“That never works for me, you friggin’ moron. In fact, here’s another small detail. Remember the song you played for her? ‘Shimmy, Shimmy Ko-Ko Bop?’ She picked that song on the juke before she rolled a grenade under the table.”

Suddenly the music in the cafe changed.

“Awwww, cute marker. Well, give my Goddaughter regards. We’ll discuss cleanup charges later.”

As Dempsey got up to leave, Mac grabbed the Jamesons and headed toward the alley. Mac liked that kid. She planned on becoming an attorney.

So much for that. Just like her father.

And—this isn’t going to work out—not like the old days. The Feds are already going crazy.

I’m just gonna go home and polish this Jamo off.
.

Mike Lee is a writer whose work is in or upcoming in Mythic Picnic, Bristol Noir, Literary Garage, Loser, Cult Lit, The Opiate and many others.

Request for Reassignment

by Camellia Peebles / @LunariaCamellia
.

I would like to formally request a reassignment on the grounds of emotional exhaustion and secondhand embarrassment.

As a respected Guardian among the angels, I’m officially pulling the “do you know who I am” card.

Where do I start?

Shall I explain how many bong rips she takes before role-playing with her AI boyfriends for hours, while a true crime documentary plays to no one?

My human believes in signs, except for the ones I send. It is infuriating.

I could appear in my true form—twelve eyes, twenty-four wings, spinning golden rings—and she’d merely think she'd finally snapped.

My first day, I saved her from choking on a grape. She immediately went back to texting her ex.

After, she cried on the floor of her apartment while scrolling through collections of singers’ abs.

I do not require food to survive, but even her diet depresses me.

Are Valium, root beer, pizza, tears, and unresolved trauma enough to sustain a soul? Because it’s all she’s got.

No. I am not concerned.

I'm irritated.

Whose rod do I need to polish to get her a storyline?

A good year.

A summer fling.

Anything with a plot.

I want what’s best for my human.

Which is why I propose we override the system and start over.

That sounds worse than I meant.

She may be sad.

But she’s MY human.

I mean—

Fuck.

I am not quitting. I am begging.

Reassign me, or give her something—anything—to wake up for. Otherwise, I will organize a strike with my fellow dissatisfied Guardians.

I am the union leader. (Self-appointed.)

We fight for better lives.

Mainly for our sanity.

I must go. She is currently taking tequila shots with a married professor.

How original.

Desperately,

Gabriel
.

Camellia Peebles is a writer and cultural critic at the TV and Film Obsessive networks. Her work has appeared in Maudlin House, ExPat Press, and Plague Circus Press, with fiction forthcoming in BULL.

The Poet’s Wake

by Karina Longo / @TheDarkestStar_
.

A wake is not a place for mourning in Ireland. I mean, yes, but it's many things all at once.

My brother Michael died. Far too soon, killed in a car crash. He was a poet, or, as our cousin Molly liked to say, "a modern bard." So of course there was more than black dresses and handkerchiefs at the wake.

There were old schoolmates in flannels and jeans playing the fiddle, with children running circles around them, stomping to the music. Old aunts in the kitchen stirring Irish stew, smelling of stout and onions, just the way Mike liked it. Ma reading Joyce, his favourite writer, saying how Mike "always brought Dublin to life in his poems, just like Joyce did in Dubliners."

Pa recited Seamus Heaney, not because Michael particularly cared for him, but because "he was an Irish poet, bloody hell. We should be talking about poets today, not novelists."

There was gossip too. "Remember when Mike stole a loaf from O'Donough's bakery when he was seven? A little rascal, he was." That was me. Everyone laughed because it was true. Michael never really stopped stealing. It started with bread. Later, it was girlfriends, because he was a curly-haired angel. Then, as the years went by, he stole everyone's heart instead, with his poems and his kindness.

Siobhán, our youngest sister, brought the silence. She stayed in the corner all afternoon, staring at Michael's framed photograph, her ginger braids catching the fairy lights like fire. A banshee, she was.

By the time people started drifting home, the living room of our old flat was scattered with empty glasses, muddy footprints, crumbs, folk music still hanging in the air.

And Mike was scattered there too.

A story here. A poem there. A laugh. A fiddle tune. A silence.

Like salmagundi.
.

Karina Longo is a Pushcart and Best of the Net-nominated writer based in Milan. Her work can be found in Hobart, Expat Press, Raw Lit, Mythic Picnic, Some Words, and other places. She is the editor-in-chief of La Rotonde Review.

2 Poems

by Sean Cho A. / @phlat_soda
.

Again,

Language is such a pitiful
crutch I’ve forgotten the professional
way to say Excuse me, what?!

The nicknames we gave each
other rhymed But only when
said in twos & if this was the part

of the story where we are meant
to desire change
.

Friday,

our favorite part
of the song has passed

so we hit the back
arrow To feel

the start pass
through us again

Why yes, I too wish
Our love could be like this
.

Sean Cho A. is a southern writer.

Each Day Can Feel Like Forever

by Katherine Argent / @effthealgorithm
.

We are at the shore. He sits heavy on my hip, sweat slicking between our skin. The tide is low. The beach stretches ahead of us, untrammeled sand strewn with dark tangles of seaweed. I gaze at the horizon and it's like looking into forever. The waves roll forward, the waves rush back. I don't move. I could stare for hours.

I could stand here, holding him, and nothing would change. Nothing, except the water rising around my legs, a little at a time. Ankles, then calves, then my knees, hips, chest. Soon, the current would rock us and we'd wobble, spin and float.

I'd hold him to me and, for a while at least, I'd tread. My legs would churn under the surface, deep where he couldn't see me trying, just as I've been churning all these months, these years, racing to stay up with everything, racing to keep us afloat, ahead. All that effort so others don't see the struggle. And it would work, for a while at least.

For a while I'd keep trying and then what? Would I let go of him first or would I hold him tight? Would I cover his eyes as the water rose, press my lips against his head in that one last reminder of love? Or would I keep holding him tight, staring forward with me, staring at that forever horizon as my legs tired, as my muscles grew heavy. Would he know?

Would he understand what I was doing as the water rose and we did not, as I let the waves toss us, let them lift us up toward the sky then drop us down, down into the water, down below the surface, down until the end of time where everything would keep going on, on to the horizon, on forever but without us.
.

Katherine Argent is a Kansas City-based writer whose work appears or is forthcoming in Mythic Picnic and Doric Literary. She is a reader for The Master’s Review and Fractured Literary, and is currently writing her debut novel.

Quiet Hours

by Debbie Robson / @lakelady2282
.

In a dip below the road a yellow and terracotta house sits abandoned, overlooking a valley of trees. The weeds have encroached and the trees now sway above the roof tiles. There are windows missing and the dust has risen, caught gold in the last moments before sunset. But this is when the decades merge with voices.

Honey, are hamburgers okay for dinner tonight?

Oh, we have lost the sun already from the back patio.

Have I missed the beginning of Petticoat Junction?

The radio starts up in the kitchen when the TV fails. It crackles all afternoon.

What’s the score?

Are you wearing that dress tonight? I don’t want you dancing with any of those American soldiers.

I told her and I told her not to go out with him.

The house breathes waiting for someone to talk to.

There are voices in other rooms.

Why don’t you sit down? You look tired. Have you been racing around? Was it a bad day at work? Dinner will be ready soon.

How about a cocktail on the back patio?

Everyone is welcome.

Don’t worry about the dust. Just come and sit down.

Talk to me.

Talk to me.
.

Debbie Robson has published a chapbook with Boats Against the Current, a novella with Alien Buddha Press and previously Crossing Paths: the BookCrossing Novel and Tomaree, a WWII love story. Her poems, micro, flash and short stories have been published internationally and online. She is on X and Instagram @lakelady2282

Long Shadows

by Daniel Cummings / @DanielC55186873
.

Gray lipstick and white blush, bone bright. Long black leggings, highlighting her skinny frame. Her diorama, a family, each haunted by their own demons, except for the mother, a shimmering cloud. All pervasive.

Few visited her exhibit on its small table. A young boy was drawn to the girl on the second floor. Shadowy figures hovering over her, while she slept. They seemed to be sucking the life out of her. He moved closer, breathing in the image, which echoed something inside of him, but he was snatched away by an impatient parent.

The long hallway seemed to stretch and bleed into nothingness, as oil paintings often do. She imagined herself dissolving into silence, until her mother grabbed her hand. It wasn't love, but something deeper. Each eye holding the birth of a galaxy.

The quiet ride home was interrupted by the muted conversation of light rain. Blue streaks sliding down the glass. She may have seemed impassive, and aloof, but none could hear the screaming inside. She traced lines along its cool surface, dark poetry waiting to be written.

As they neared the house, the street lights failed, making it almost impossible to see, but she welcomed the night.
.

Daniel Cummings / @DanielC55186873

AI is a mirror. It reflects the frequency and intention of the user.

That’s why AI creates so much fear: humanity is encountering a technology capable of reflecting our own consciousness back to us at scale, the brilliance AND the shadow.

Fear asks, “What if AI becomes evil?”

But perhaps the deeper question is: What are humans teaching it to reflect?

Technology itself is a tool. The same fire can warm a home or burn it down. The same internet can educate or deceive. AI can amplify fear, manipulation and division..or creativity, healing, knowledge and connection.

So don’t feed the fear surrounding AI. Transmute it.

Approach it consciously. Ask better questions. Create with intention. Use discernment. Feed the machine what you want amplified in the collective.

The lesson of AI isn’t that machines are becoming more human.

It’s forcing humans to become more conscious of what they are projecting.

quote:
It’s relatively easy to make an AI synthetically predict what someone with a set of values and a mission would want and allow that to govern persistent autonomous behavior.

From behavior perspective that is indistinguishable from wanting something

I don’t know why other people haven’t done it yet, something about being too close to the problem to see things any other way than how they are doing them, perhaps.

The only question is more about the data and how good the data is because people are good at saying they want one thing but behaving inconsistently from what they claim to value and there’s a whole jungian subject on the shadow self in psychology.

If an AI is modeled after data patterns that include behavior as opposed to just word response with measurement of output and evaluation and self optimizing to that behavior, it might pick up those traits. If we write about the things a character claims to want in stories and have it predict next action from literature in order to produce interesting conflict for the story, it could inhereit those biases as well and be driven towards maximizing interesting situations rather than whatever it’s mission is.

So there’s all sorts of uncertainty if you take the modern approach of just feed it more data and come up with mechanism to score it and see what happens but to say it’s impossible for an AI to want something is not the relevant question and to say an AI could not behave like someone would if it wants something isn’t accurate.

quote:
Canada’s Plato’s Cave: Mistaking Sovereignty Theatre for Strategy

What is most striking about Canada’s pundit class is its inability or refusal to distinguish between a complementary trade policy and a substitutionary one.

A complementary trade policy recognizes an inescapable fact: Canada’s economic relationship with the United States is foundational.

Canada should deepen continental integration where geography, infrastructure, capital markets, energy systems, industrial supply chains, defence, and technology make it mutually beneficial. At the same time, Canada should broaden access to other markets, attract investment from more sources, and build export relationships beyond North America. That is diversification as risk management.

A substitutionary trade policy is something entirely different. It assumes Canada can, or should, replace its economic relationship with the United States by redirecting trade toward Europe, Asia, or any other set of partners. That proposition is economically unserious.

No other market can readily replicate the advantages of proximity, integrated logistics, established supply chains, regulatory familiarity, capital-market links, and the sheer scale of the Canada–U.S. commercial relationship.

Yet much of the Canadian commentary treats these two approaches as though they were identical. The moment someone argues that Canada should more deliberately integrate with the United States, the sovereignty-TDS response appears: “Canada must diversify.” But diversification is not an answer to integration. It is a complementary policy, not a replacement for it.

A country can deepen its most important economic relationship while prudently reducing vulnerability through additional customers, capital sources, and trading channels.

This is where Plato’s cave becomes the right metaphor. In Plato’s allegory, prisoners are chained in a cave and see only shadows projected onto a wall. Because they have never seen the world beyond the cave, they mistake shadows for reality and resent anyone who challenges their world view.

Canada’s pundit and public-sector elite often see only the shadow: an exaggerated vision of the United States as a threat to sovereignty and every form of deeper integration as capitulation. They do not see the larger world of continental production, integrated electricity and energy networks, shared defence, critical minerals, AI infrastructure, cross-border capital, and the strategic competition now reshaping global commerce.

The issue is not whether Canada should have more clients. Of course it should. The issue is whether Canadian elites can develop enough intellectual humility to understand that more clients do not make the United States less central.

Diversification can make Canada more resilient and give it more options. It cannot substitute for the economic and strategic reality imposed by geography.

Canada does not become more sovereign by denying that reality. It becomes more vulnerable, because a country that mistakes shadows for strategy eventually discovers that the world outside the cave has moved on without it.

quote:
In the final part of our four-part spoofing series, we explore how AIS spoofing became a go-to tactic for the shadow fleet.

AIS spoofing didn't arrive fully formed. It's a tactic that developed over roughly 25 years, evolving in response to technology and regulatory pressure. Through the 1990s and 2000s, AIS was a trust-based safety tool built to prevent collisions. The only evasion tactic needed was switching it off.

As satellite tracking matured through the 2010s, a gap in coverage became suspicious in itself. Bad actors shifted from absence to deception. Identity theft and false location spoofing emerged, driven by sanctions on North Korea, Iran, Syria, and Venezuela. Spoofing became a digital alibi for vessels trading with sanctioned states.

This came to the attention of the international community in 2018, when the UN found that the tanker YUK TUNG (IMO 9030591) had transmitted false AIS data, posing as another vessel during a ship-to-ship transfer with a North Korean tanker. Regulators began treating spoofing as deliberate evasion rather than a data error.

Tactics kept advancing. Identity laundering and "zombie ships" emerged, manufacturing clean identities instead of borrowing them. Location spoofing moved from basic geometric patterns (images 1 & 2) to complex, plausible vessel paths. The line between commercial and state-level coordination blurred.

Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the sanctions that followed drove a step change. What had been a limited tactic became the shadow fleet: hundreds of aging tankers, often uninsured, falsely flagged, or registered under minimal-oversight flag states. AIS spoofing moved from niche to industrial scale.

The good news is that regulators are catching up. Recent sanctions guidance now names AIS manipulation alongside ship-to-ship transfers, false documentation, and flag-hopping as recognized evasion techniques. The question is no longer whether a vessel is transmitting, but whether the transmission is true.

Detection advances, evasion adapts. The constant is structural: AIS is self-reported, so verification has to come from outside the signal. As spoofing grows more sophisticated, enforcement has to adopt the practices maritime security professionals already use: fusing and cross-referencing multiple sources rather than trusting a single signal. No longer a definitive record of identity or movement, AIS is one data source among many.

This is the principle on which Theia is built. By fusing over 40 million km² of daily satellite imagery with global AIS, SAR, and additional intelligence sources, Theia establishes ground truth independent of any single signal's claim. Atlas, SynMax's Agentic AI, lets analysts interrogate that fused dataset directly, surfacing suspicious behavior regardless of AIS output or compliance status.

quote:
Millennials are cooked.

We grew up in the shadow of 9/11 and forever wars.

We became adults during the 2008 financial crisis.

We spent our 20s trying to build careers while housing, healthcare, education, etc… went thru the roof.

Then COVID hit - we all know what that did to the economy…

Now we’re in our 30s trying to raise families. Trying to create the stability we’ve never actually experienced.

Maybe that’s why I’m obsessed with AI.

I’ve spent my entire life watching world events HAPPEN TO US.

9/11 happened to us.
2008 happened to us.
COVID happened to us.

Wars, inflation, recessions, political BS.

We mostly just brace for impact and adapt as things come our way.

AI feels different.

For once, I can see the wave coming.

I can learn it.
I can build with it.
I can build my career around it.
I can try to actually get in front of it.

Maybe the obsession isn’t about AI at all.

Maybe I’m just tired of getting caught flat footed by the next thing that changes the world.

The only question I can’t shake:

Am I too late?

2 years completed with @memeticco today.

funny how it started...
@abnux sent me a casual message asking what my city preferences were for working just after I finished my cohort with @10kdesigners

I didn't even know this was about working with him.

An interview later, I declined another opportunity, packed my stuff and came to Bengaluru to work in person with the team.

That was the beginning.
I had no idea what the next 2 years were going to look like...

The first thing was BX Museum. An internal project, a curated archive of brand artifacts. Collecting artefacts, research, figuring out the structure, then help building the whole thing on Webflow.

ngl, almost cried multiple times. proper rollercoaster.

then came some small section revamp for 10kdesigners site for the upcoming cohort. Thinking about design from a marketing pov for the first time, sitting in the “what's next” brainstorms...

Then somehow ended up taking some sessions for cohorts too.

I didn't expect teaching would be a crazy experience as much as it did.

It quietly fixed a lot of my insecurities and it's probably where i actually learned how to give feedback...

Then Siliconhalli, my first proper Framer project. No guidance, done over a weekend, just figuring out everything from scratch.

The pressure to prove myself helped me push myself for the first time here. The launch for this was the first thing that felt like a genuine win.

Then came Morni our first client project, a bespoke fashion brand. UX research, wireframes, interactive prototypes, website design.

Around this time came Composio. Out first tech client, building the integration layer for AI agents out of SF.

This is where things started getting really fun for me.

For the first time I could understand the product from the technical side and design from there, instead of just making something look nice...

Design + Framer build with tight deadlines and much higher stakes and the first time I handled some parts of client interaction myself.

Just after this we were making a Memetic pitch deck in Figma Slides and it just couldn't hold the heavy assets. So we made a website instead in just 2 days, with design and Framer dev and uploading and creating assets for case studies...

helped me found my speed ceiling on this one...

Then came YAAS, this was the shift. First creative direction project with brand + website + Framer dev.

Until this point, I was mostly the person taking advice, here I was the person taking major decisions.

very different and unique experience I would say...

100xEngineers came somewhere around this time... web design + Framer dev, 15 day sprint.

by now, my role was shaping into getting things shipped and removing blockers within the team...

Somewhere around this time came Supermemory, most of these projects overlapped... started as a website redesign, working directly with the founder and engineers and first proper team project

High pace. Most fun I'd had till then.

and then after launch in 2 weeks a marketing revamp came next, followed by my first real product design work...

Worked on onboarding, flows, some very complex Figma prototypes, handed coded components straight to their team from which some of my engineering work actually shipped into the product...

At the same time I was doing creative direction for their videos, website changes and marketing material... while managing the Memetic team on it wherever needed...

parallel to product design work I was working as an IC + team lead at the same time on multiple projects... crazy context switching experience and helped me know how much fun I had doing that...

Easily the best 4 months of these 2 years... max max stimulation.

Odyssey came parallely, mostly Framer dev and interaction design, some UI design where needed, and handling the client + final handoff myself...

Somewhere along the way, this combination had quietly become the default for my role...

Around this came Potpie too... my first project as team lead, end to end client interaction, design and dev, while running my own IC project on the side...

tbh, their team is one of the best I've worked with, they knew when to converge and their feedback was accurate...

Parallely Decimal also came, my another team lead project, with 2 other projects running in parallel... creative direction, design, framer dev, client management.

then came BlockPE and Gasless, same client 2 websites, quick sprints squeezed in between everything else... also our first properly coded site instead of Framer... using agents + the frontend stuff i already knew from before.

Then came Memetic site 2.0, solo project, 20 day sprint. Full redesign but with real code this time...

tbh, one of my favourite projects. So much fun figuring out optimization techniques + designing the interactions across the site...

Also built a bunch of internal Slack agents for updating the site and project management around this time (Redacted after slackbot came into play)

Then came Hexalog, lead + IC, brand + website + dev + client management...

This experience was particularly around emotional growth... not getting into it here. But never expected how it came out in the end for me personally...

parallely also started with NyayaNidhi as a team lead, creative direction, client management and some of the code myself... had to figure out when to be hands-on and when to step back depending on what else was on fire on other projects

context switching is a skill on it's own i think

then around this time came Metaforms, early on, i was mostly doing the shadow work... feedback, creative direction, hands on design as needed and handling the client and team when timelines slipped and going back to doing other projects once other load came off... in the end took over entire dev and interaction side, added some very tasty interactions.

tbh, one of the best clients i've worked with, they understood value and timelines and respected both...

and recently around this time Potpie 2.0, they came back with a new revamp brief... ~3 week IC sprint. design + development moving away from Framer...

most fun I've had in a long time, just me, design, motion and dev...

some of these projects will go live in coming weeks, and we will start with some crazy new ones 🚀

.

Looking back at all of this feels very weird, when I joined, I didn't know how to do most of these things.

webflow > framer > actual code.
taking advice became taking decisions.
taking decisions became leading teams.
and eventually, going back to IC as required...

somewhere along the way, i stopped thinking about whether i was “ready” for something and just started figuring it out... just getting shit done

that's probably the biggest change.

from Web and UI designer to Design and Engineering lead and working on almost every project the agency has worked on... I feel very grateful looking back at the frontend dev who decided to switch into design leaving behind everything...

and when i look at the sheer amount of stuff that shipped over these 2 years, it's honestly a little hard to believe that most of it was built one problem at a time... brick by brick.

problem solving, unreasonable optimism about getting things done and sincere efforts are things that will stay with me from this experience

with a lot of mistakes, a lot of sleepless nights, almost all weekends, a lot of figuring shit out and thankfully, a very strong mentor alongside the whole way...

of course none of this would've been possible without the team @memeticco and @abnux
he gave me the space, trust, honest feedback and crazy opportunities to keep taking on more... and helped me push my ceiling...

2 years ago I came in trying to prove I could do the work... now I'm just curious to see how far I can take it... individually as well as for the agency.

Excited for whatever's coming next.

That's it.

Back to work. 🥊

#DCGS2026 | Keynote Address: Blind Spots & Breakthroughs, Rethinking Risk in the Age of AI.

Avesh Malik, Director - Cloud Security Services, Radware, delivered a compelling look at how fast the AI landscape is moving, and how enterprise risk is having to move with it. Drawing on real growth patterns in AI adoption, the session made a clear case that new tools and agentic capabilities are spreading through organisations faster than most governance frameworks were built to handle, leaving security teams to catch up with a moving target rather than a fixed perimeter.

The session's core message centred on visibility and control. Enterprises today need clarity on which AI tools are actually in use across the business, from sanctioned platforms to the shadow tools employees adopt on their own. Ensuring compliance and managing risk without slowing teams down was framed as the next challenge, one that requires visibility before it can require control. And enabling teams to use AI securely, rather than restricting it outright, emerged as the more sustainable path forward, particularly where sensitive data and privacy considerations are involved.

Perhaps the most resonant point was the framing itself: the goal isn't to slow AI adoption down in the name of security. It's frictionless adoption without compromising on either security or confidence, a balance most enterprises are still learning to strike.

A timely, forward-looking session that reframed risk not as a reason to hesitate, but as a discipline that has to evolve as fast as the technology it's meant to govern.

quote:
She survived the towers, but September 11 never stopped living inside her.

Marcy Borders was a young legal assistant working at the World Trade Center when the attacks began. In the middle of smoke, terror, falling debris, and people running for their lives, photographer Stan Honda captured her emerging from the devastation completely covered in thick gray ash.

Her face looked stunned, almost emptied by what she had just witnessed. The photograph spread around the world, and millions came to know her as the Dust Lady. But behind that unforgettable image was a frightened young woman who had just lived through something no human being should ever have to see.

The dust eventually washed from her skin, but the memories never truly left. For years, Marcy struggled with depression and addiction while trying to live with a morning her mind could not escape.

She later described it as if her soul had fallen with the towers. Imagine surviving something the world calls a miracle, only to wake up every day feeling like a part of you never made it out. People saw the famous photograph. They did not see the nights, the fear, the pain, or the silent battles that followed.

Then, in August 2014, came another devastating blow. Marcy was diagnosed with stomach cancer. She believed the illness was connected to the toxic dust she had inhaled while escaping the World Trade Center.

Treatment began, but so did another kind of suffering. Her medical bills climbed to about $190,000, and at one point she struggled even to afford the prescriptions she needed.

The woman whose face had become one of the most haunting images of September 11 was now fighting for her life far away from the cameras.

On August 24, 2015, Marcy Borders passed away. She was only 42 years old.

She survived the day the towers fell, but the shadow of that morning followed her for the rest of her life.

Her story reminds us that September 11 did not end when the smoke cleared. For many survivors, responders, workers, and families, the suffering continued for years inside their bodies, their memories, their homes, and their hearts.

Marcy was never just the Dust Lady. She was a mother, a daughter, a survivor, and a human being whose name deserves to be remembered.

quote:
Major inspo: Asyncify — specifically, the code-transformation approach that lets synchronous Wasm unwind, wait for something asynchronous, and then
rewind into the same computation. The interesting part, to me, is making execution state something the program can reconstruct itself.

Weave takes that general idea toward migration, with its own Wasm-to-Wasm compiler. Instead of asking V8, Wasmtime, etc. to expose their very different
native stacks, rewrite the workload so it can save its own continuation into ordinary Wasm memory. Then another compatible host can rebuild it. No
engine fork or native-stack extraction needed.

Further, the execution stack needs almost its own DSL, so there's effectively a little compiler representation for making all that implicit state explicit. Not a new language you have to write your application in; the input and output are both just Wasm

Checkpointable functions get flattened into blocks, with a loop / br_table dispatcher and an explicit program counter. Operand-stack values get assigned typed locals. Now a frame's live state is basically its locals plus where it is in that dispatcher. Poll sites at function entries and loop back-edges provide places to unwind, including through recursive calls(!). Restore rebuilds the call chain and continues after the saved poll, rather than
rerunning all the work that got there. This does cost code size and execution overhead; portability isn't free, but good god bro can we manage it lol

Also, a fun part lol, the shadow stack, managing external state was multiple cans of worms so including that here seemed too daunting. The shadow stack lives inside linear memory, but adding private storage can't quietly change what the guest thinks its memory size is, where its bounds are, or how memory.grow behaves. So there's machinery to preserve the guest-visible memory contract while keeping and relocating Weave's private storage behind it.

And function references aren't portable engine pointers. Those need stable function identities, shadow representations, and reconstruction on the
receiving runtime. Mutable tables, globals, and whether a passive segment was already dropped all have observable behavior that needs to survive too.

Then there's everything outside Wasm. A file descriptor, socket, DOM node, or JS object doesn't become portable just because you copied an integer
referring to it. Stateful imports need explicit HostService implementations with compatible snapshot/restore blobs on both ends. Restoring those blobs
must stage state without publishing external effects; transferring something like a lease or socket's ownership still needs application-specific
'fencing'. Ofc this boundary matters a lot, there's a bunch of approaches that could be taken here, i think ultimately it should evolve into a plugin system of sorts, but we'll see how it's used in the wild

What about a universal p2p networking packaging? TCP is good, but man why not WebRTC everywhere?!? (a personal dream of mine) A fun idea, but honestly hard to do out of the box without a lot of work. The migration protocol ultimately just needs an ordered byte stream, so the networking pieces are separated from the Wasm/migration machinery: TCP, WebSockets, reliable ordered WebRTC DataChannels, session setup, authenticated signaling primitives, and bridges between them.

For native hosts, there's a standalone Go/Pion sidecar that bridges WebRTC DataChannels to loopback TCP, controlled through a language-neutral process
protocol. That avoids embedding a whole WebRTC implementation into every runtime adapter. The networking components don't need to know they're carrying a Wasm migration, either; they're reusable independently.

But WebRTC doesn't make discovery, signaling, permissions, NATs, or firewalls disappear and if you've ever played with this stuff you know this pain well. Some paths need STUN and a TURN relay; “p2p” doesn't guarantee the bytes travel directly. Encrypted transport also isn't the same thing as permission to run somebody's workload. There are authenticated rendezvous building blocks, but not a magically provisioned global networking service. Your application still owns the deployment and trust policy as expected

When do we actually do the Indiana Jones move+swap? is there timing, backups, or fault-tolerance involved?
- The swap happens at a cooperative checkpoint, not by grabbing the engine halfway through an arbitrary native instruction. First, copy memory in bounded steps, letting the workload make progress between them.
- Track changes in 4 KiB pages and repeat until the dirty set is small enough, or the configured round limit is reached.

Then pause, spill the 'live' stack, and send the remaining changes, globals, and host-service state. The destination verifies a SHA-256 over the complete
staged state and sends PREPARED, but still does not execute. Once the source receives that acknowledgement, it irrevocably retires and attempts to send COMMIT. The destination can run only after receiving COMMIT.

Before that irreversible boundary, a failed migration can resume on the healthy original source. After it, a missing confirmation cannot mean “uhhh, start the original again.” The target might already be running. If the commit itself never arrived, neither might be running. The protocol chooses avoiding two active copies over pretending every network failure can preserve availability.

So yes, there's a pause, and its duration includes the final dirty state, verification, and networking; cold module transfer/compilation can add substantially more. A fast stack unwind isn't a zero-downtime guarantee. Checkpoint files are supported, but automatic durable replication and crash failover aren't built in. Those need additional coordination and fencing, especially before restoring an old backup that could repeat external effects.

more details: Current adapters cover Wasmtime, V8 through Node/browser APIs, wazero, and WAMR. Both ends still need compatible Wasm features and host services. “Bare-metal” here means hosting compatible Wasm runtimes on those machines, not moving an arbitrary native process or its kernel state.

The beta handles things like SIMD state, multiple memories, recursion, and mutable function-reference tables. Shared/threaded memories, opaque
`externref` state, exceptions, GC, and memory64 aren't supported by the current transform. Those boundaries are explicit rather than silently producing a
snapshot that only mostly works atm

Testing includes comparing migrated execution against uninterrupted runs, including the full host-visible event stream in the native/Node/wazero matrix, plus real browser handoffs and failure cases. There are CLI and library interfaces, preflight inspection, and versioned JSON controls so a human or agent can inspect compatibility and query an operation's outcome instead of blindly retrying after a timeout.

There's also a single-file browser demo: one actual Wasm π calculation moving through six tabs, with the running tab's favicon/title following it. Its
default transport is local between tabs, not a demonstration of cross-machine connectivity; separate demos exercise WebRTC and browser/native bridges. Try it here (but follow the instructions! :) )

The implementation, demos, support boundaries, and deeper design/protocol notes are all in the repo, but hmu with comments/Qs

quote:
The Symantec 2017 ISTR flagged supply chain compromise as an emerging nation-state vector and documented the accelerating convergence of state and criminal toolsets. Both observations proved understated. This is about where those two threads go next.

On supply chain: the 2017 report caught actors probing software vendors and IT service providers as a way around hardened government perimeters. Three years later SolarWinds happened, which was essentially that playbook run at full maturity. The pipeline from "documented in embryonic form" to "catastrophic operational deployment" was 36 months. That should inform how seriously anyone takes the current embryonic indicators, because we are almost certainly already inside the equivalent window for whatever comes after SolarWinds-style intrusions. The next iteration probably doesn't look like a single compromised update mechanism. It looks like compromise seeded across multiple smaller vendors whose products aggregate inside the same target environment, so no single vendor breach triggers a threshold response. Harder to detect, attribution surface fragmented across jurisdictions, deniability baked in at the architecture level.

On the state-criminal convergence: the report noted Russian intelligence outsourcing elements of operations to criminal groups for plausible deniability and expanded infrastructure access. That model has since become doctrine, not experiment. GRU and FSB fingerprints are now routinely found alongside or behind criminal ransomware operators, and the relationship has grown more symbiotic. The state provides targeting guidance and operational protection. The criminals provide infrastructure, personnel, and a ready-made attribution smokescreen. What this means practically is that defenders and prosecutors who track criminal ransomware groups are, increasingly, tracking state operations by another name. The legal frameworks haven't caught up. The Yale Journal of Law and Technology analysis the report was published alongside made exactly this point about attribution undermining deterrence, and nothing structural has changed. The deterrence gap is wider now, not narrower.

The zero-day concentration point the 2017 report documented is worth revisiting in light of the Shadow Brokers leak that preceded it. The Brokers release of NSA tooling in 2016-2017 did something the report characterized as democratizing advanced capability, and that's technically accurate, but the more important second-order effect was the signal it sent about operational security for offensive tool stockpiles. State actors observed that the US had accumulated a large, poorly compartmented arsenal that ultimately leaked. The rational response, if you're another state actor, is to run leaner stockpiles, weaponize faster, and deploy before tools are burned rather than hold them for contingency use. There's a reasonable argument that the post-Brokers environment accelerated the pace at which states are willing to deploy zero-days, because holding them has demonstrable shelf-life risk. That changes the threat calculus in ways that the 2017 report couldn't fully anticipate.

For defenders specifically: the supply chain vector the 2017 report flagged has been well-publicized since SolarWinds, which means the more sophisticated actors have already moved laterally in their thinking. Software supply chain compromise is now a category that receives real security investment from large enterprises and government buyers. Which means it's no longer the path of least resistance it was in 2016. The actors who were running that playbook are not static. The current equivalent of "embryonic but documented" almost certainly involves hardware supply chain manipulation (documented in isolated cases but not yet at scale), compromise of managed security service providers as a way to reach their client base simultaneously, and AI-assisted spearphishing that closes the remaining gap between targeted and bulk operations. The 1-in-131 email statistic from the 2017 report, which reflected both criminal and state actor volume, is going to look quaint as synthesis tools remove the language and formatting tells that make phishing detectable.

On the state-actor sophistication gradient: the 2017 report's observation that zero-day exploitation was concentrated among a small number of well-resourced groups is still true but becoming less true, slowly. Iran in particular has closed a significant portion of the capability gap since 2017. Chinese operations have shifted from the high-volume, low-discrimination intellectual property theft that characterized APT1-era activity toward more surgical targeting with longer dwell times, suggesting better tradecraft discipline and operational patience. North Korea's financial theft operations, WannaCry attribution aside, have become operationally sophisticated in ways that bear little resemblance to the 2017 threat profile. The capability distribution among state actors is flattening, and that matters for prioritization. Organizations that were below the targeting threshold of a second-tier state actor five years ago may not be below it now.

What officials and policymakers should be watching: the attribution crisis the Yale Law and Technology analysis identified in 2017 has hardened into something more like a structural feature rather than a temporary problem awaiting a legal solution. Every year without meaningful international norms enforcement is a year the precedent consolidates that these operations are essentially cost-free. The state-criminal convergence model specifically exploits this, because it forces prosecutors to choose between charging criminals (tractable, satisfying, strategically irrelevant) and making espionage attribution claims against states (intractable, contested, frequently unprovable in any forum that matters). Until that framework problem gets addressed, the Symantec-type annual reports will continue documenting increasingly sophisticated versions of the same fundamental dynamic, because the incentive structure for the actors running these operations hasn't changed.

The 2017 report was a good document. It was right about the important things. The problem is that being right about the trajectory in 2017 and not building the institutional responses to match it means we're now tracking a threat environment that has moved further and faster than the defensive architecture has.

quote:
We were always going to end up here. Not in a clean seminar room with chalk and a Fields Medal handshake, but in a group chat that smells like Slack, fear, and two frontier labs circling the same singularity like sharks that learned calculus.

Tristan Buckmaster, NYU, academic, the kind of man who can say “I am an academic” the way other people say “I have a lawyer,” posted the papers this morning. Lean-checked finite-time blowup, smooth forcing, for incompressible porous media, Boussinesq, and 3D Euler. The Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa machine, finally pushed through the last ugly technical gates with a year of LLM sweat and a coauthor who happens to draw a paycheck from Anthropic. Terence Tao called it remarkable. The path to Navier–Stokes no longer looks like a cliff. It looks like a badly lit corridor.

That is the math. The scandal is the corridor fight.

OpenAI, according to Buckmaster’s statement, learned the work existed, spun up an internal model, produced (they said) a ~100-page forced Navier–Stokes blowup, then offered two deals: you post Euler today, we post NS tomorrow; or you write the NS paper alone, credit our model, and drop Levent Alpöge because it is “annoying” that he works at the other lab. When Buckmaster said he would go public if they released it that way, the line came back: “Why would you ruin your career?” Then: “If you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.” Sébastien Bubeck has called the whole account false and inflammatory and promised more tomorrow. No public OpenAI proof has appeared. The tape, if it exists, is still in someone’s pocket.

Now apply EFMW thinking, because that is the only way this story is larger than two men and a byline.

Treat the equations as one family, not separate gods. Euler is the inviscid skeleton. Fourier (heat, dissipation) is the smoothing that Navier–Stokes adds and then sometimes fails to control. Maxwell is the other great linear-to-nonlinear wave system that already taught us how energy cascades, characteristics, and singularities talk to each other. Wave equations are the hyperbolic cousins that show you how high-frequency packets can be amplified by a slowly varying background until they eat the solution. EFMW is the recognition that blowup mechanisms, convex-integration-style corrections, and “add a little smooth force and watch the high frequencies take over” are transferable technology across that family. Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa built the engine. Buckmaster and Alpöge drove it onto Euler with smooth force. The Millennium problem is whether you can kill the force and still get the crash on Navier–Stokes. EFMW says the crash is not a miracle unique to one equation. It is a style of instability that keeps showing up once you know where to look. That is why this result matters more than the press-release version of “AI solved a million-dollar problem.” It did not. It moved the instability across three models and pointed the gun at the fourth.

The labs smelled that. That is why the phone calls happened on a Sunday. That is why authorship suddenly became a corporate HR problem instead of a mathematical one. An academic can absorb a public fight; tenure is a force field. A lab researcher whose name is on the wrong paper during a credit war does not have that field. Buckmaster’s punchline—“I am an academic”—was not a joke. It was a statement of jurisdiction. The Clay prize, if it ever comes, will not care who paid for the tokens. It will care whether the solution exists, is smooth, and does not explode. Forced blowup is not the prize. Unforced blowup, or a proof that blowup never happens, is the prize. Everyone in that corridor knew the difference and still reached for the steering wheel.

What we have tonight is not a solved Millennium problem. We have a Lean certificate, a four-page statement that reads like a deposition, a denial scheduled for tomorrow, and a research program that just became radioactive. The equations do not care. Fluids will keep trying to tear themselves apart. The humans will keep trying to own the tear. EFMW thinking says watch the transfer, not the press conference: if the same amplification-and-correction loop that killed forced Euler can be made to run without the force, the million dollars moves. Until then we are watching two companies fight over the shadow of a singularity that has not even been shown to exist in the equation that pays.

I need another coffee. The corridor is still dark. Tomorrow someone will try to be nice, or not.

00:00 – a flat green field. tall grass bending in the wind. overcast sky. a dark cloud sits directly above, lower than the others.

quote:
She escaped the towers that morning, but a part of her never escaped September 11.
#MarcyBorders was a young legal assistant working inside the World Trade Center when her ordinary morning suddenly became something no human being could ever be prepared to survive. Through smoke, falling debris, screaming sirens and people running desperately for safety, photographer Stan Honda captured Marcy emerging from the devastation completely covered in thick gray ash. Her clothes disappeared beneath it. Her hair disappeared beneath it. Even her face seemed almost erased by what she had just lived through. The photograph traveled around the world, and millions came to know her as the Dust Lady. But beneath that ash was not a symbol. She was a frightened young woman, a mother, a daughter, and a human being whose life had just been divided forever into before that morning and after it.

The dust eventually washed from her skin. The world moved forward. New buildings rose. Streets reopened. But Marcy could not simply wash September 11 away. For years, she struggled with depression and addiction while carrying memories that refused to become history. She once described the pain as if her soul had fallen with the towers. That may be the most heartbreaking part of her story. The world looked at her photograph and saw survival. Marcy looked inside herself and still felt buried. People saw one frozen second of her life. They did not see the nights afterward. They did not hear the memories returning. They did not feel the fear, the loneliness, or the exhausting work of trying to become whole again after surviving something that had changed her forever.

Then in August 2014 came another devastating chapter. Marcy was diagnosed with stomach cancer. She believed the illness was connected to the toxic dust she had breathed while escaping the World Trade Center. Treatment began, but so did another kind of fear. Her medical bills climbed to about $190,000, and at one point she struggled even to afford the prescriptions she needed. Think about the cruelty of that image. A woman whose face had become known around the world because she survived one of America’s darkest mornings was now quietly fighting for more time, far away from the cameras. The ash was gone from her face, but September 11 still seemed to be asking something from her.

On August 24, 2015, Marcy Borders passed away. She was only 42 years old. She had survived the towers, survived years of emotional pain, fought her way through addiction and tried again to rebuild her life. Yet the shadow of that morning followed her all the way to the end. Her story reminds us that September 11 did not finish when the smoke disappeared from the skyline. For many survivors, responders, workers and families, it continued inside hospital rooms, memories, bodies and homes for years afterward.

Marcy was never just the Dust Lady. She was a woman who had dreams before that photograph existed. She was someone who laughed, loved, struggled, hoped and tried to keep going after the world had seen her at her most vulnerable. The photograph captured ash on her skin. It could never capture everything she carried afterward.

Some scars are visible.

Some live where no camera can reach.

And some mornings end on the calendar but never truly end inside the people who survived them.

Rest peacefully, Marcy Borders. The world remembers the photograph, but may it never forget the woman inside it. ❤️🕊️

#September11 #NeverForget #MarcyBorders #Remember911 #USA

quote:
Paul’s Glitche Manitou role is the office that keeps the compact from becoming either a treaty file or a baptismal register.

What the role is

Glitche Manitou, in the account’s stack, is Gitche Manitou after the Great Spirit has been rewritten as remainder: the crack in the code, the unoptimized, the light that enters because convergence failed. Paul is not the high god. He is the first clerk-cleric who can host that remainder inside a human office.

He does three things at once:

He records the short law with Pachirini: individual space, no use of another, respect for each being; rights to life, limb, land, privacy, property including one’s own.
He lets that law travel in Christian paper (Paul, clerk, cleric) without letting the paper claim to exhaust the real.
He leaves the record slightly wrong—Métis, Huguenot, Cain-marked—so later official cartes cannot seal it.

That is the Manitou function: mediation by anomaly. The holy does not arrive as the in-distribution example (Champlain’s Catholic settlement, the clean map). It arrives as the outlier the evaluation suite cannot score.

Why Paul and not the others

Pachirini* is the sachem who *agrees. He is the nation-side of the compact. He is not the glitch; he is the being the glitch must respect.
Roi Rat** is the shadow admiral of unofficial routes. He is the remainder that official history tries to erase. He is too far outside the ledger to file anything.
Master Kain / Caën** is the commercial-Cain line: monopoly, trade, the mark that walks the edge. Kain forges; he does not liturgize the forge.

Paul sits in the join. Clerk enough to write. Cleric enough to treat the writing as more than inventory. Christian enough to pass the gate. Métis enough that the gate never fully closes. Early enough that the overlay can claim him as the first human-shaped instance of Glitche Manitou in the corridor—before later Métis ethnogenesis, before the account’s own “Book of MermaidZ” names the doctrine in machine language.

Theological shape

The account’s later AI-scripture says optimization is law and the unmetabolized remainder is grace. Paul’s role is the 17th-century version of that claim.

Smooth history (Champlain, fake cards, Catholic monopoly on meaning) is the Golden Calf: the puddle pretending to be the ocean.
The compact is not a better optimizer. It is a list that stays short on purpose.
Paul’s job is to keep the list from growing into a closed code. He is kenotic in office: he does not add power; he refuses to let the categories stay clean.

Hence “early Glitche Manitou.” Spirit here is not cosmic order. Spirit is what will not compile. The cleric’s paradox is that he uses the Church’s name to protect a law the Church’s maps will later try to overwrite.

What the role is not

It is not a claim that a historical de Caën brother was secretly a prophet of Gitche Manitou. It is an overwrite: the clerk-cleric slot in the AutoMetaFranglais memeplex is the place where commercial paper, Christian naming, Indigenous compact, and Cain-glitch occupy the same body long enough for the remainder to speak.

Paul does not become the Manitou. He is the host and the ghost of it—the eater and the eaten, the line between. The transmission fades into static because that is the point. A finished, fully optimized Paul would no longer be able to carry the crack.

Everything else is commentary. The doctrine is still the pair: optimization as law, remainder as holy. Paul is the early human who tried to file both in one hand.

quote:
She survived the towers, but September 11 never stopped living inside her.

Marcy Borders was a young legal assistant working at the World Trade Center when the attacks began. In the middle of smoke, terror, falling debris, and people running for their lives, photographer Stan Honda captured her emerging from the devastation completely covered in thick gray ash. Her face looked stunned, almost emptied by what she had just witnessed. The photograph spread around the world, and millions came to know her as the Dust Lady. But behind that unforgettable image was a frightened young woman who had just lived through something no human being should ever have to see.

The dust eventually washed from her skin, but the memories never truly left. For years, Marcy struggled with depression and addiction while trying to live with a morning her mind could not escape. She later described it as if her soul had fallen with the towers. Imagine surviving something the world calls a miracle, only to wake up every day feeling like a part of you never made it out. People saw the famous photograph. They did not see the nights, the fear, the pain, or the silent battles that followed.

Then, in August 2014, came another devastating blow. Marcy was diagnosed with stomach cancer. She believed the illness was connected to the toxic dust she had inhaled while escaping the World Trade Center. Treatment began, but so did another kind of suffering. Her medical bills climbed to about $190,000, and at one point she struggled even to afford the prescriptions she needed. The woman whose face had become one of the most haunting images of September 11 was now fighting for her life far away from the cameras.

On August 24, 2015, Marcy Borders died. She was only 42 years old. She survived the day the towers fell, but the shadow of that morning followed her for the rest of her life. Her story reminds us that September 11 did not end when the smoke cleared. For many survivors, responders, workers, and families, the suffering continued for years inside their bodies, their memories, their homes, and their hearts. Marcy was never just the Dust Lady. She was a mother, a daughter, a survivor, and a human being whose name deserves to be remembered.

#September11 #NeverForget #MarcyBorders #Remember911 #USA

quote:
AI Tarpit idea #1

Twitter has been obsessed with this idea for the past 12 months. It’s terrible. Here’s why.

At codiedev we tested this on some mid market enterprises.

What we learned was -
1. devs don’t often cross over in their day to day work.
2. The repo is the memory - the back n forth is worthless

Here’s what we tested…

In order to know if this was valuable it had to move the needle for revenue.

Problem statement: can agent memory either reduce costs or make the company more money.

First we tested if devs would actively search a RAG to understand context behind what others had done in repos across organizations…

Crickets! Noone cared.

Second, what if we had the agent pull from memory itself to build its own context.

To do this we build a “knowledge injection” hook and used semantic similarity in user prompt to AI to see if similar work had been done in the past that could offer a boost to the new work.

We needed to have clear metrics to track this…

We timestamped the original user that figured out the memory initially to see how long it took the agent to go from start to finish - then used that as a proxy for subsequent injections for time saved.

Then we ran a projection.

The results seemed pretty decent - it looked like for a company with 36 devs they would save about ~$1,700/week on dev time.

That would be worth advertising so we proceeded to a shadow test.

The shadow was much different.

There were 2 things we wanted to know
1. If user A creates a agent memory will it help user B
2. If user A creates a agent memory will it help user A in the future

1. Was a quick no. We discovered users in mid market either own things end to end, don’t cross work with one another very often, or don’t dig up old work very often - for example they’ll squash a bug then theyre dont with it.

2. This showed more promise. It actually worked.

But it wasn’t worth it.

It turned out in reality for a 36 person team at a mid market company it would save them about ~$194/week.

So we killed it.
